basis: The query is the whole ABSTRACT of paper1, describing the motivating problem (implicit writing norms are hard to externalize/apply), the proposed solution (two writing support concepts reifying document/sentence-level distributions), and summarizing the user study findings (N=16, participants revised structure/content and gained confidence). Candidate [0] is paper2's ABSTRACT, playing the identical structural role: it states the motivating problem (difficulty understanding commonalities/variances across API code examples), introduces the proposed system (EXAMPLORE, an interactive visualization/synthetic code skeleton), and summarizes the lab study results (helped users answer more questions correctly and explore unfamiliar APIs). Both are single-paragraph abstracts serving as the paper's top-level summary of problem, approach, and evaluation outcome -- the clearest same-role match, more so than the Introduction [1] or Conclusion [20], which serve expanded or concluding roles rather than the concise abstract role.

The query is paper1's whole Introduction, which motivates the problem (junior researchers lack examples of implicit writing conventions), surveys the gap in existing approaches, introduces the proposed system (CorpusStudio) with its key features, previews the user study (N=16), and lists contributions. Candidate [1] plays the exact same role in paper2: it motivates the API-learning problem, discusses gaps in existing resources/tools, introduces EXAMPLORE and its key features, previews the user study (16 Java programmers), and lists contributions. Both are whole INTRODUCTION sections serving the same structural and rhetorical function in their papers, even though topics (writing support vs. API usage) differ.

The query is paper1's whole "Background and Related Work" section, which surveys prior research on writing norms/learning and writing support tools to situate the paper's contribution relative to related work. This plays the same structural role as paper2's whole "RELATED WORK" section (index 2), which surveys prior work on interfaces for exploring collections, API learning, and API usage mining to situate EXAMPLORE relative to related research. Both are top-level related-work sections comparing the paper's approach to multiple strands of prior work and are further broken into subsections (candidates 3,4,5 are paper2's subsections of this same section, but the query itself is the whole-section, so the whole-section candidate 2 is the closest correspondence, even though the query also has finer background subsections not fully mirrored in paper2).

The query is a Related Work subsection motivating the problem space (why community/API writing norms matter and how newcomers learn them) before introducing the paper's tool. The closest role match in paper2 is candidate [4] 'Learning APIs with Code Examples', a Related Work subsection that similarly motivates why learning API usage (analogous to learning writing norms) is hard and how developers currently try to learn it (via examples, search, documentation), setting up the paper's tool as filling the gap. Both are foundational motivating subsections about learning norms/practices of a community/domain, not about the technical mining or visualization mechanics. Other candidates (mining/visualization related work [5], or interfaces [3]) address different sub-topics not matching 'why norms matter and how newcomers learn them'.

The query is a Related Work subsection (2.2) that positions the paper's approach relative to prior tools/research on writing with external/corpus text, drawing distinctions and connections to specific prior systems (IntroAssist, Naeem et al., Hui and Sprouse). This plays the same role as paper2's whole RELATED WORK section [2], which similarly surveys prior interfaces/tools (Sifter, WordTree, OverCode, API mining techniques) and explains how EXAMPLORE builds on or differs from them. Both are the paper's comprehensive related-work discussion contrasting the new system against closely related prior approaches. While paper2 also has finer-grained subsections (3,4,5) that map to sub-parts of its related work, the query itself is a single subsection covering two closely related sub-topics (retrieved/generated text and corpus-based text), making it best matched to the encompassing RELATED WORK section as a whole, which plays the analogous consolidating role. No single narrower subsection in paper2 covers exactly this combined role as well as the full section does.

The query is a Related Work subsection critiquing how existing tools/search engines fail to support writers finding relevant examples (topical search vs. need for specific analogous snippets, context-switching issues), motivating the paper's integrated approach. This plays the same role as candidate [4] 'Learning APIs with Code Examples', which is a Related Work subsection explaining how prior research on code example search, quality, and comprehension shows limitations (developers search but face limited time/attention, existing search doesn't surface the right granularity of examples), motivating EXAMPLORE's approach to help users explore examples more effectively. Both are the specific 'why existing example/search tools fall short for the paper's particular support goal' subsection within a larger Related Work section, contrasting with other related-work subsections that discuss visualization interfaces (candidate 3) or mining/visualization techniques (candidate 5), which serve different roles.

The query is the whole "Corpus Studio" section (section 3) of paper1, which describes the system's design goals, walkthrough scenario, and detailed feature/implementation subsections (text editor, document-level norms via PDC, sentence-level retrieval, user notes, tooltips, plagiarism-avoidance features, and implementation stack). This is a broad system-description section combining motivation, a usage scenario, feature design, and implementation details all in one. In paper2, no single section covers this same combined scope as tightly as candidate [1] INTRODUCTION does for motivation, but the query is clearly a system-description section, not an introduction. Looking at paper2's structure, the closest functional counterpart -- a section that introduces and describes the tool's core concept, design, and how it works for the reader, similar in role to describing 'what the system is and how it functions' -- is the SYNTHETIC CODE SKELETON section [6], which explains the core design concept and rationale of EXAMPLORE's central artifact. However, the query also includes a walkthrough scenario (like candidate [7]) and implementation details (like candidate [8]). Since the query is a single top-level section combining scenario + design + implementation, and paper2 splits these into three separate sections (SYNTHETIC CODE SKELETON, SCENARIO, SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AND IMPLEMENTATION), the single paper2 section that plays the most similar overarching role -- introducing the core tool concept and its design rationale, which the query centers on -- is the SYNTHETIC CODE SKELETON section, with secondary correspondence to the SCENARIO and IMPLEMENTATION sections for the walkthrough and technical details respectively.

The query is a "Design Goals" subsection that articulates the high-level motivating goals guiding the development of the paper's interactive tool (Corpus Studio), explaining what the tool should empower users to do. In paper2, the closest role-equivalent content is the INTRODUCTION section, which similarly motivates the problem and lays out the design rationale and goals for EXAMPLORE (e.g., giving a bird's-eye view of API usage, allowing drill-down to concrete examples). While paper2 lacks a dedicated "Design Goals" subsection, the INTRODUCTION performs the same role of stating the guiding objectives behind the tool's design before describing its implementation, making it the best match. No other candidate (e.g., SYNTHETIC CODE SKELETON, SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE) focuses on abstract design goals in this way.

The query is a walkthrough scenario describing a persona (Alice) using CorpusStudio to explore its interface features step by step while drafting a paper (inspecting section titles, retrieving sentences, bookmarking, continuing to write). This plays the exact same role as candidate [7] 'SCENARIO: INTERACTING WITH CODE DISTRIBUTIONS', which presents a persona (Victor) walking through EXAMPLORE's interface features step by step (viewing highlighted examples, filtering by constructor options, exploring guard conditions) to illustrate practical usage of the tool. Both are usage-scenario narratives demonstrating the tool's interaction model through a fictional user, rather than describing implementation, related work, or evaluation results.

The query is a subsection (3.3 "System Characteristics") of paper1 that comprehensively describes CorpusStudio's design features (text editor, document-level and sentence-level norm surfacing, spatial retrieval, rendering modes, notes, tooltips, anti-plagiarism features) and their theoretical grounding (Variation Theory, Structural Alignment Theory). This plays the same role as paper2's "SYNTHETIC CODE SKELETON" whole section [6], which describes EXAMPLORE's core design/visualization feature (the code skeleton) and its theoretical/empirical grounding (drawn from studies on API learning barriers, e.g., Duala-Ekoko and Robillard, Ko et al.). Both are the central 'system design and rationale' section of their respective papers, describing the main interactive artifact's structure and the cognitive/theoretical motivations behind its design choices. While EXAMPLORE's paper also has separate architecture/implementation sections ([8]-[11]) and a walkthrough scenario ([7]), the closest single counterpart in role -- describing the system's design features and theoretical foundations -- is the SYNTHETIC CODE SKELETON section, which similarly interleaves feature description with theoretical justification.

The query is an "Implementation Details" subsection describing the concrete technical infrastructure (web framework, database, deployment specs) used to build the paper's system. In paper2, candidate [8] "SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AND IMPLEMENTATION" plays the same role: it explains the pipeline/technical implementation (data collection via mining framework, MongoDB storage, rendering) of EXAMPLORE. Both are technical-implementation sections describing infrastructure choices for the tool, rather than motivating the problem, presenting results, or reviewing related work. The subsections under it ([9],[10],[11]) cover specific pipeline phases (data collection, post-processing, visualization) which are narrower than the query's general infrastructure description, so the whole-section [8] is the closer overall match in role.

The query section describes how paper1's corpus (papers) was collected and processed through a data pipeline (collection, sentence splitting/labeling, embedding, clustering) to build the CorpusStudio system's backend data. This plays the same architectural/implementation role as paper2's 'SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AND IMPLEMENTATION' section, which describes EXAMPLORE's three-phase pipeline (Data Collection, Post-processing, Visualization) for collecting and processing code examples into the system's data structures. Both sections explain the end-to-end data pipeline underlying their respective interactive tools, covering collection, normalization/processing, and preparation for the interface. While the query's content spans data collection and processing sub-topics that individually resemble candidates 9 (Data Collection) and 10 (Post-processing), the query as a whole most closely corresponds to the entire architecture/implementation section [8], which itself bundles collection, processing, and visualization-prep steps together.

The query describes a low-level, technical data preprocessing step (splitting manuscripts into sentences via NLTK/LLM approach, saving metadata) in a "Data & Processing" section of paper1. Paper2's closest analog in role is its "SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AND IMPLEMENTATION > Post-processing" subsection (index 10), which similarly describes normalizing/canonicalizing raw mined data (chained calls, variable names) into a structured form and storing metadata (start/end indices) for use in the interface. Both are mid-pipeline data transformation steps that convert raw source material into structured, annotated units for downstream visualization/use. No other candidate addresses this granular preprocessing role -- Data Collection (9) is about initial mining/extraction rather than sentence-splitting/normalization, and Visualization (11) is about rendering, not preprocessing.

The query describes a specific technical sub-step of data processing (embedding sentences with a specific model/parameters to enable spatial retrieval) within a larger data/processing pipeline section. The closest analog in paper2 is candidate [10] 'Post-processing', which similarly describes the concrete technical sub-step of normalizing/canonicalizing mined code examples into a form usable by the visualization, sitting as a subsection within the larger 'SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AND IMPLEMENTATION' pipeline (paralleling paper1's 'Data & Processing' section). Both are the middle processing stage that transforms raw collected data into a form usable for the tool's core interactive/retrieval functionality, following a data-collection stage and preceding a visualization/retrieval-use stage. Candidate [9] (Data Collection) is about initial mining/collection, not the transformation/embedding step, and [11] (Visualization) is about rendering/UI updates rather than data preparation, making [10] the best role match.

paper1_subsection_name: Extracting an Ordered Distribution over Section Titles
basis: The query describes a specific technical subsection detailing how raw data (section titles) is processed/clustered/canonicalized into a normalized, structured form (ordered distributions with counts) for visualization in CorpusStudio. This mirrors the role of paper2's 'Post-processing' subsection [10], which describes how EXAMPLORE normalizes and canonicalizes raw code examples (chained calls, variable names) into a canonical form with distributions stored for visualization. Both are the middle 'processing' stage between raw data collection and final visualization rendering, converting messy raw instances into a clustered/canonicalized distributional representation. The alternative candidate [8] (whole SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE section) covers the full three-phase pipeline including collection and visualization too broadly, whereas the query is narrowly about the clustering/processing step itself, matching the Post-processing subsection's scope most closely.

Both are the top-level "User Study" section describing the overall experimental design: within-subjects methodology, study procedure/protocol, task structure, and rationale, serving as the umbrella section under which participant details, methodology, and API/task selection subsections sit. Candidate [12] plays this same overarching role for EXAMPLORE (introducing the within-subjects design, task rationale, and study procedure), just as the query section introduces CorpusStudio's within-subjects design, tasks, and procedure. The query's content also touches on participant recruitment and methodology (paralleling candidates [13]-[15]), but as a whole-section query it most centrally corresponds to the whole 'USER STUDY' section [12] rather than any single subsection.

The query is a 'Participants' subsection of a User Study section, describing who was recruited (16 participants) and their characteristics (background, experience level). Candidate [14] plays the exact same role: it is the 'Participants' subsection of the USER STUDY section in paper2, describing the 16 recruited participants and their Java programming experience/background. Both are participant-description subsections within an otherwise analogous user-study section structure.

The query is the 'Study Procedure' subsection detailing the step-by-step protocol (training, tasks, conditions, timing) used to evaluate CorpusStudio against a baseline. Candidate [15] 'Methodology' plays the identical role in EXAMPLORE's user study section: it describes the within-subjects design, counterbalancing, session structure (training, task 1, task 2, post survey), and control vs. experimental conditions. Both are procedural walkthroughs of how the study session was run, distinct from participant recruitment (candidate 14) or API/task selection rationale (candidate 13).

The query is a "Qualitative Results" section reporting themes and participant insights derived from qualitative analysis (grounded theory coding, affinity diagramming) of a within-subjects user study comparing a tool to a baseline. In paper2, candidate [18] "Qualitative Analysis" plays the analogous role: it reports themes from coded free responses in the post survey (filtering feature popularity, complaints about search, workflow fit ideas, etc.), derived from qualitative coding of participant responses. Both sections serve as the qualitative counterpart to a quantitative results section, presenting participant-derived themes and insights about tool benefits/limitations. While the query is broader (covering multiple sub-features like section titles and sentence retrieval), its core role -- presenting qualitative themes from user study analysis -- matches [18] most closely, more so than the quantitative-focused [17] or the whole RESULTS section [16].

The query is a qualitative-results subsection reporting participant perceptions and usage patterns of a specific feature (section title distributions) drawn from user study data, including quotes and behavioral observations. In paper2, the closest role match is the RESULTS section (index 16), which similarly synthesizes qualitative and quantitative findings from the user study, including participant quotes, coded free-response patterns, and observations about how users perceived and leveraged EXAMPLORE's features (e.g., filtering, distribution counts, structure for learning). While index 18 (Qualitative Analysis subsection) is a narrower candidate that also reports coded free-response themes and quotes similar in style to the query, the query's whole-subsection role of thoroughly documenting a single feature's perceived value, usage patterns, and participant quotes across multiple sub-numbered paragraphs most closely mirrors the full RESULTS section's blend of quantitative and qualitative reporting on EXAMPLORE's reception. Given the instruction to prefer the most centrally representative candidate, the whole RESULTS section (16) is chosen as it encompasses both survey-based and behavioral evidence of feature perception, paralleling the query's comprehensive treatment of the section-title-distribution feature.

The query is a qualitative-results subsection reporting participants' reported benefits and usage patterns (via quotes, participant IDs, coded themes) for specific interface features in a user study — this is the same role played by paper2's 'Qualitative Analysis' subsection [18], which similarly reports coded free-response themes, participant quotes (P3, P4, P7, P16, etc.), and usage patterns/benefits of specific EXAMPLORE features (filtering, color-coding, exploring examples) drawn from the post-survey. No candidate in paper2 addresses writing-support or sentence-level features specifically, but by role (qualitative user-study findings on feature usage/benefits) [18] is the clear structural analog.

The query is a subsection reporting a specific qualitative finding from a user study (how participants used a particular feature—bookmarking/notes—during their task), drawn from post-study interviews/free responses. The closest role match in paper2 is the 'Qualitative Analysis' subsection of RESULTS, which similarly reports specific qualitative findings from participants' free responses about how they used and valued particular interface features (e.g., filtering, color-coding) during the study, including participant quotes. Both serve as detailed, feature-specific qualitative evidence sections within a larger Results/Findings section, rather than being about study design, quantitative results, or system implementation.

The query is a fine-grained qualitative-results subsection reporting how study participants used and evaluated a specific UI feature (tooltips) via post-hoc participant quotes and usage patterns. Both are subsections under a broader results section that analyze qualitative participant reactions to particular tool features, rather than quantitative correctness metrics (covered elsewhere, e.g., [17] Quantitative Analysis). The closest topical area in paper2 is the qualitative analysis of user study results (candidate 18) or results section (16), but these discuss filtering features, interface usability, and workflow fit—not plagiarism or originality safeguards. Both play the role of presenting statistical/survey-based evidence of the tool's effectiveness and usage patterns for a specific task, as opposed to the qualitative free-response analysis (candidate 18) or the overall Results section (16). There's a secondary tie to candidate 16 (whole Results section) since it contains both quantitative and qualitative content, but the quantitative-specific subsection [17] is the closer role match.

The query is paper1's Discussion section, reflecting on conceptual and empirical insights from the CorpusStudio study plus its limitations. Candidate [19] 'DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS' plays the exact same role in paper2: it reflects on what the EXAMPLORE study results reveal about benefits/trade-offs and explicitly discusses limitations (bug-free examples, stale/low-quality examples, sorting criteria). Both sections synthesize study findings into broader design insights and acknowledge scope/limitations, distinguishing them from the more narrowly empirical Results sections (16-18) which report study data without this reflective, limitations-focused framing.

The query is a Discussion subsection from paper1 (CorpusStudio) analyzing how study participants interpreted 'relevance' of retrieved sentences relative to their writing goals -- a reflective, qualitative discussion tied to a writing-support/text-retrieval tool. Paper2 (EXAMPLORE) is about API usage example visualization, and its closest analogous sections are DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS [19] and the Qualitative Analysis of results [18]. However, these sections discuss EXAMPLORE's trade-offs between expressive power/visual complexity, code quality assumptions, and API familiarity effects -- not the notion of 'relevance' of retrieved content being dynamically constructed based on user goals versus semantic similarity, which is a domain-specific insight about information retrieval relevance criteria for writing support that has no counterpart in EXAMPLORE's discussion of code skeleton visualization. Paper2 does not perform any retrieval/relevance-matching function comparable to CorpusStudio's sentence retrieval, so no candidate plays the same conceptual role.

paper1_subsection_name: Designing a System with Many Retrieved Examples
basis: The query is a discussion subsection reflecting on trade-offs of presenting many (N=25) retrieved examples at once, including cognitive load vs. learning benefits and visual rendering support for pattern recognition. This most closely corresponds to paper2's DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS section, which similarly reflects on the trade-off between EXAMPLORE's expressive power (showing many examples/features at once) and visual complexity/cognitive overload, and calls for future work on presenting information in a visually simple yet comprehensive manner. Both are meta-level reflections on the design decision to show many examples simultaneously and its trade-offs, rather than being a specific results or implementation section.

paper1_subsection_name: Designing Writing Support for and with Community Integration, not AI Integration
basis: The query is a discussion subsection arguing that the paper1 system's design philosophy deliberately avoids AI-generated text in favor of surfacing community-vetted corpus examples directly, framing this as a "community integration, not AI integration" design choice with implications for onboarding and discoverability. None of the EXAMPLORE candidates play this role. EXAMPLORE's DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS section (19) discusses trade-offs of visual complexity, quality of mined examples, and sorting criteria, but never contrasts itself against AI-generated writing assistants or frames its approach as valuing 'community' quality standards versus AI training corpora -- that specific philosophical positioning (non-AI, community-sourced, peer-reviewed corpus) has no counterpart in EXAMPLORE's paper, which is about visualizing API usage examples rather than writing support tied to community norms. No candidate addresses this specific design-philosophy argument, so there is no genuine match.

The query is a Discussion subsection from a different paper (about a writing-support tool embedding metacognitive strategies like reverse outlining and learning from examples in a sidebar UI) reflecting on how its design relates to prior work on metacognition in interaction. None of the EXAMPLORE paper2 candidates play this role: EXAMPLORE has no Discussion subsection about embedding metacognitive strategies into an interface -- its closest section 'DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS' (index 19) discusses trade-offs of visual complexity, generalizability, and code quality assurance, not metacognitive strategy design or self-reflection support. The topic, framing, and citations (Tankelevitch et al., reverse outlining) are entirely specific to the other paper's domain (writing assistance) and have no counterpart among EXAMPLORE's sections, which focus on API usage visualization, mining, and evaluation. Therefore no candidate corresponds by role.

Both are the paper's "Discussion/Limitations and Future Work" section, reflecting on the scope and generalizability of user study findings and proposing directions for future research. Candidate [19] 'DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS' plays this exact role in paper2, discussing trade-offs, current limitations (e.g., not guarding against stale/low-quality examples, sorting criteria), and future improvements, paralleling the query's discussion of study scope limitations (participant background, corpus, task duration) and future research directions.

The query is the paper's Conclusion section, summarizing what the system (CorpusStudio) contributes and the broader interaction model it exemplifies. Candidate [20] plays the identical role for EXAMPLORE: it is the CONCLUSION section, recapping the system's contribution (synthetic code skeleton, drill-down to examples), summarizing evaluation results, and gesturing to future work/broader implications. Both are whole-section, final-summary conclusions rather than results, discussion, or related-work sections, making this the clear structural and functional match.
